The fog had been thick for three days, a gray wool that swallowed the world whole. Elias Thorne, the keeper of the Blackwood Point Lighthouse, had grown accustomed to the isolation, but the silence of the storm was different. It wasn’t the roaring absence of sound; it was a heavy, pressurized quiet that made his ears pop.

Elias climbed the 142 spiral stairs, his boots clanging against the iron treads. At the top, in the lantern room, he adjusted the Fresnel lens. The beam cut through the mist, a solid pillar of white light sweeping the dark water. He was checking the oil levels when he noticed it.

It wasn’t a ship’s horn. It wasn’t the crash of waves against the rocks. It was a rhythmic, low-frequency hum that seemed to vibrate through the floorboards and into his bones. *Thrum... thrum... thrum.*

Elias paused, his hand hovering over the wick. He pressed his ear against the cold glass of the lantern room. The hum was coming from the sea, but it didn’t sound like water. It sounded like a machine.
